intro: The best stain for a wood fence is Ready Seal, an oil-based penetrating semi-transparent stain that sprays on evenly, hides lap marks and fades instead of peeling. Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck gives more color control, BEHR Solid rescues old mismatched fences, and DEFY Extreme is the water-based pick.

A fence is often a bigger job than a deck: a 150-foot privacy fence six feet tall has about 900 square feet per side before posts and rails. Vertical wood is easy on finishes, though, so ease of spraying and even fading matter more than squeezing out extra durability. That is how the seven picks below are ranked.
quickAnswer: Buy Ready Seal for most wood fences. Choose Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck for custom colors, Olympic Maximum for big-box value, BEHR Premium Solid Color for old or patched fences, DEFY Extreme for low-VOC states, Cabot Australian Timber Oil for cedar showpieces and Thompson's WaterSeal for utility fences. Expect three to five years from a semi-transparent stain on vertical boards.

If you are finishing a deck at the same time, the floor needs a tougher product; see our [best deck stain rankings](/best-deck-stain-reviews/) and pick a matching tone.

sections.h: The 7 Best Stains for Wood Fences in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: Rankings draw on manufacturer data sheets and labels, stated spray and coverage guidance, VOC availability and recurring owner feedback on how each product goes on and ages on fences. No weathering trials were run for this guide. Sprayability and even fading carried the most weight, because they decide how a fence job goes.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: Ready Seal Exterior Wood Stain and Sealer

blocks.p: Ready Seal is the fence stain owners most often pass along to neighbors, and the reason is how easily it goes on. The maker says it needs no back-brushing and leaves no lap marks, and fence owners back that claim up more consistently than for most products.

It is an oil-based penetrating stain that sprays smoothly through a pump sprayer or an airless rig, which is what you want over hundreds of pickets. It fades rather than peeling, so a maintenance coat a few years on is a cleaning and one more pass. Tones run from light natural shades to deeper browns, and the semi-transparent look suits both cedar and pressure-treated pine. Five-gallon pails are common and bring the cost per gallon down. Two things surprise first-timers: the color looks light when wet and deepens over about two weeks, and it needs warm, dry weather to cure. It will not soak through old solid stain or paint.
**Pros:** no back-brushing or lap marks per the maker; sprays easily; fades evenly instead of peeling; wide range of natural tones; economical five-gallon pails.
**Cons:** color develops over about two weeks; oil-based cleanup and slower dry time; not suited to going over old film finishes.

blocks.h3: Best Pro-Grade: Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck Semi-Transparent Stain

blocks.p: SuperDeck is the Sherwin-Williams exterior wood stain line, and its semi-transparent version is a common contractor choice for fences, decks and siding. Buying at a paint store helps on a fence job: staff can tint a wide range of colors, match a previous batch for touch-ups and suggest the right sprayer tip.

The line comes in oil-based and waterborne versions, so you can choose based on your state's VOC rules and how much drying time you can tolerate. Owners commonly report even color and good longevity on vertical boards. The waterborne version dries faster, which shrinks the window for overlapping passes, so work in shade and keep a wet edge; the oil version is more forgiving on long runs. It costs more than big-box brands and is only sold at Sherwin-Williams locations, though frequent sales narrow the gap. For a fence that is part of the look of the house, the color control is worth it.
**Pros:** tinted and color-matched in store; oil and waterborne versions; wide custom color range; made for decks, fences and siding.
**Cons:** higher price than big-box brands; waterborne version needs care to avoid lap marks; only sold at Sherwin-Williams stores.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sherwin-Williams+SuperDeck+semi-transparent+stain&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Big-Box Value: Olympic Maximum Stain and Sealant in One

blocks.p: Olympic Maximum Stain and Sealant in One is the flagship exterior stain at Lowe's, and for many fence owners it is the most practical buy. It is easy to find, tinted in store and priced below most paint-store brands.

The line covers clear, transparent, semi-transparent and solid versions, so you can pick the look that fits your fence and change it later without switching systems. The label promises water repellency and mildew resistance, and owners generally report good results on vertical surfaces. It can be sprayed, but a quick back-brush or back-roll keeps lap marks away, especially on smooth boards. Because it behaves somewhat like a coating, heavy coats stacked over the years can build up; keep coats thin and recoat only when water soaks in. On cedar and redwood it looks a touch less natural than penetrating oils. For a typical pressure-treated or cedar privacy fence, it is a solid value.
**Pros:** widely available with in-store tinting; clear through solid versions; water repellency and mildew resistance per the label; moderate price; sprayable with back-brushing.
**Cons:** can build up with repeated heavy coats; less natural look than penetrating oils; needs back-brushing to avoid lap marks.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Olympic+Maximum+stain+and+sealant+in+one&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Old Fences: BEHR Premium Solid Color Waterproofing Stain and Sealer

blocks.p: When a fence has seen better days, BEHR Premium Solid Color is the product to reach for. Solid stain hides gray weathering, replacement boards, old blotches and the green tint of treated lumber, giving the whole run one even color.

On vertical surfaces, solid stains outlast semi-transparent ones, and owners frequently report several years before a recoat. It is an acrylic sold and tinted at Home Depot, so colors are plentiful and touch-up cans are easy to find, and it cleans up with soap and water. People looking for a review of BEHR stain on fences mostly report the same pattern: good results on a clean, dry fence, and peeling where it went over an old penetrating stain that still repelled water or onto damp wood. That is a prep issue, not a formula flaw. It hides the grain completely, so it is the wrong pick for a new cedar fence you want to show off. Plan on two coats for even color.
**Pros:** hides weathering, patches and mismatched boards; wide color range at Home Depot; long life on vertical surfaces; soap-and-water cleanup.
**Cons:** hides the grain completely; can peel over old penetrating stain or damp wood; usually needs two coats.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BEHR+Premium+solid+color+waterproofing+stain+and+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Water-Based: DEFY Extreme Semi-Transparent Wood Stain

blocks.p: DEFY Extreme Semi-Transparent is a water-based stain that combines pigment with zinc oxide nanoparticles to resist UV, which makes it a strong answer to the question of which fence stain offers good UV protection without solvent.

For fence projects its strengths are cleanup and availability: tools wash with soap and water, odor is low and it ships to states where many oil stains are restricted. It penetrates rather than forming a thick film, so wear shows as fading, not peeling, and the tones work on cedar, redwood and pressure-treated pine. The challenge on a fence is drying speed. Fast drying helps with short weather windows but makes lap marks more likely, especially in direct sun. Spray or roll in shade, work one section between posts at a time and back-brush as you go, and avoid days when dew or rain will arrive before it sets. Owners commonly report good color retention on vertical boards, with a slightly flatter look than oil.
**Pros:** soap-and-water cleanup and low odor; zinc oxide for UV resistance; fast drying; sold in strict VOC states; penetrates rather than building a film.
**Cons:** fast drying makes lap marks likelier in sun; needs warm, dry conditions; can look flatter than oil stains.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEFY+Extreme+semi-transparent+wood+stain&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Cedar Showpieces: Cabot Australian Timber Oil

blocks.p: Cabot Australian Timber Oil is a translucent oil-based finish that brings grain forward and adds a rich, warm color. It was designed with dense hardwoods in mind, but on fences it shines on new cedar, horizontal slat designs and hardwood privacy screens where the wood is a feature rather than a backdrop.

Because it penetrates rather than forming a film, it fades gradually and can be refreshed after cleaning, and it is stocked at major retailers. For a basic pressure-treated privacy fence it is more product than you need, and other stains here cost less per gallon. On a modern horizontal cedar fence or an entry screen, the depth of color is the reason to buy it. Test the tone on a spare board first, since some shades read orange on pale cedar. Apply thin coats, back-brush and wipe excess on smooth faces. Expect slower drying than water-based options and solvent cleanup.
**Pros:** rich, warm translucent color; penetrates soft and dense woods; widely available; no film to peel; shows off cedar and hardwood grain.
**Cons:** costs more per gallon than basic fence stains; some tones read orange; slower drying.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cabot+Australian+Timber+Oil&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget: Thompson's WaterSeal Waterproofing Stain

blocks.p: Many fences do not need a premium product, and Thompson's WaterSeal Waterproofing Stain is the budget answer. For a back-lot fence, a dog run or a utility fence behind the garage, it adds color and water repellency at a low price and is sold in almost any hardware store.

It comes in transparent, semi-transparent and solid versions, and the more pigmented ones last longer in sun. Owners generally report that it goes on easily with a pump sprayer or roller and repels water well when fresh. The tradeoff is life. On a sunny fence, expect to recoat sooner than with the premium stains above, and the transparent version offers limited UV protection. Avoid overlapping heavy coats, which can look uneven, and recoat only when water soaks in. Spend more on the fence that faces the street and frames the house; for the rest, this is a sensible way to protect wood without overspending.
**Pros:** low price and sold almost everywhere; transparent, semi-transparent and solid versions; easy sprayer or roller application; good water repellency when fresh.
**Cons:** shorter life than premium stains; lighter versions give less UV protection; heavy overlapping coats look uneven.

sections.h: How Is Fence Stain Different From Deck Stain?

blocks.p: Most fence stains are the same products sold for decks, often labeled for decks, fences and siding together. What changes is which features matter. A deck needs abrasion resistance and must survive standing water. A fence needs to go on fast over a huge vertical area, look even from twenty feet away and stay presentable for years with little attention.

Thin penetrating oil stains flow through pump and airless sprayers easily and tolerate overlapping passes without dark stripes. Thicker acrylic and solid stains can be sprayed but usually need back-brushing or back-rolling. If you plan to spray, buy a product the label says can be sprayed.
On a fence, lap marks show as darker bands where wet stain overlapped stain that had started to dry. Oil-based penetrating stains are much more forgiving than fast-drying water-based ones.

A penetrating stain that fades evenly can be refreshed with a cleaning and one coat. A film-forming stain that peels needs scraping or stripping on every picket, which is miserable on a long fence. Unless the fence is old and mismatched, favor penetrating products.

Fences usually hold their color longer than decks, so a fence and deck stained the same day will drift apart a little over time. For other wood around the yard, such as pergolas and siding, see the [best exterior wood sealers](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/).

sections.h: Transparent, Semi-Transparent or Solid: Which Fence Stain Should You Choose?

blocks.p: Semi-transparent is the right opacity for most fences. Transparent suits new cedar and redwood you want to show off; solid suits old or patched fences.
These add a hint of color and show nearly all the grain. They have the least pigment, so they fade fastest, but on a vertical fence they can still go two to three years.
The best default. On new pressure-treated pine it hides the green tint and blotchiness of treated lumber, and on cedar it evens out board-to-board color.
Solid stain hides grain and behaves like a thin paint. It lasts longest on vertical boards but can peel, and it commits you to that look.

Pigment is what blocks UV, so the fence stains with the best UV protection are the more heavily pigmented semi-transparent and solid versions. A south-facing fence in high-altitude sun can need attention twice as often as a shaded north side. In humid climates, choose a label that lists a mildewcide and keep sprinklers and soil off the bottom boards.

sections.h: When Should You Stain a New Fence?

blocks.p: Stain a new fence once the wood absorbs water, which for pressure-treated pine is often a few weeks in hot, dry weather and several months in humid or cool weather.

New treated pickets arrive wet from the treatment process. Stain applied too early cannot soak in; it sits on the surface or fails within months. Sprinkle water on a few boards: if it soaks in within a minute or two, the wood is ready. Kiln-dried treated lumber is usually ready sooner.

New cedar is usually drier and can often be stained much sooner. Smooth planed faces may carry mill glaze, a hard surface that blocks absorption; a few weeks of weathering or a light sanding opens it. Many cedar pickets are rough on one side, and that side takes stain best.
A new fence left bare for a full year in strong sun turns gray and may start to check, which means more prep. Aim for the first stretch of dry, mild weather after the wood passes the water test.

A mild cleaner and rinse removes dirt, sawdust, pencil marks and mill residue; let it dry a day or two. If you are building the fence, consider staining pickets before installing them. Spraying both faces flat on sawhorses is faster and reaches spots that are hard to hit later, such as where pickets cross rails.

sections.h: How Do You Prep an Old or Gray Fence for Stain?

blocks.p: Repair first, then clean, brighten, deal with any old finish and let the wood dry for at least two days.

Push on every post to find loose or rotted ones at the ground line, replace broken pickets and reset popped nails. Post rot at or just below grade is the most common failure on older fences, and staining a fence that is about to fall over wastes stain.

Spray on an oxygen-based wood cleaner and give it time to loosen gray fibers, mildew and dirt. Rinse at low pressure with a wide tip, nozzle well back from the boards, working with the grain. Then apply an oxalic acid brightener, which restores color, neutralizes the cleaner and removes dark iron stains around fasteners. On cedar and redwood the difference is striking.

If water soaks in everywhere, a penetrating stain can go right on. If old solid stain or paint is peeling, scrape or strip it, or switch to a solid stain over the sound areas. A penetrating stain cannot get through an intact film.
Allow two dry days after washing, then test a few pickets with a water drop. Once water soaks in within a minute or two, start staining.

Board-on-board and shadowbox fences hide faces from the sprayer, so angle into the overlaps from both sides and expect to use 15 to 25 percent more stain. Horizontal slats have upward-facing edges that hold water; give them an extra pass. Split-rail fences need generous stain on post bottoms and rail ends. Stain all six sides of gate boards where you can.

sections.h: How Much Fence Stain Do You Need?

blocks.p: Multiply length by height for one side, double it for both sides, and add 10 to 20 percent for posts, rails and overlapping designs. A 100-foot fence six feet tall is 600 square feet per side.

Labels often list 150 to 300 square feet per gallon on smooth wood. Rough-sawn pickets and old weathered boards drink far more, often 100 to 175 square feet per gallon, and spraying uses more than brushing because of overspray.

blocks.p: Five-gallon pails cost less per gallon and keep the color consistent. If you buy single gallons, box them, which means mixing several together in a bigger bucket before you start, so the color does not shift between cans partway down the fence.

blocks.h3: Plan for the number of coats

blocks.p: Many penetrating stains go on as one coat, or two coats wet on wet. Solid stains usually need two full coats. Buy for the label's coat count plus a little extra for touch-ups.

blocks.h3: Cost per year, not per gallon

blocks.p: A good penetrating stain that lasts four years on a fence costs less over time than a bargain product you reapply every year, especially once you count the weekends.

sections.h: Should You Spray, Roll or Brush Fence Stain?

blocks.p: Spray for speed, then back-brush or back-roll each section to push stain into the grain. That combination gives the best result on most fences.
The simplest tool for thin penetrating stains. Cheap, easy to clean and fine for fences up to a few hundred feet. Use a fan tip, hold it close to limit drift and keep a brush ready for runs.

Much faster on long fences and able to handle thicker stains, with more overspray, so masking and wind matter more. Use a tip in the size range the stain maker recommends; our [paint sprayer guide](/best-paint-sprayer/) covers models that handle exterior stain.

Slower but with better control and almost no overspray. A thick-nap roller suits rough pickets and a stain pad helps on rails. A brush is essential for detail, corners and back-brushing rough-sawn wood.

blocks.h3: A sequence that avoids lap marks

ol: Start on the shaded side and follow the shade as the sun moves.
Work one section between posts at a time.
Stain picket tops and post caps first, since end grain absorbs the most.
Do rails and the backs of pickets where they meet rails, then the faces, top to bottom.
Keep a wet edge and finish each section post to post before stopping.
Back-brush or back-roll as you go.

blocks.p: Check for at least a day without rain, and avoid evenings when dew will form before the stain sets.

sections.h: How Long Does Fence Stain Last, and How Do You Protect Neighbors and Plants?

blocks.p: On vertical fences, transparent stains often last two to three years, semi-transparent three to five, and solid stains longer, depending on sun and climate. South and west sections fade first.

Each spring, sprinkle water on pickets in full sun and in shade. If it beads, the stain is working; if it soaks in quickly, clean and recoat. Penetrating stains let you redo only the sections that need it.

blocks.h3: Protect the bottom of the fence

blocks.p: Daily sprinkler spray is a leading reason fence bottoms fade, grow mildew and rot early. Adjust sprinkler heads and pull soil, mulch and plants back from the pickets so they can dry.
Talk to the neighbor before staining a shared fence; some want both sides done, others want a say in the color. Some HOAs dictate fence colors or require approval.

Spray drifts through picket gaps onto cars, siding and patios. Use drop cloths or a spray shield, skip windy days, and roll the faces near cars and windows. Cover plants with breathable cloths rather than plastic, water them first and rinse off any overspray. Keep oil stain off concrete and stone, which it marks hard; if it happens, our [concrete oil stain remover picks](/best-oil-stain-remover-for-concrete/) can help. Lay oily rags flat outdoors to dry or seal them in a water-filled metal can, because they can ignite as they cure.

mistakes: Staining a new pressure-treated fence too soon

Fresh treated pickets are still wet from treatment, so stain cannot soak in. It sits on the surface and fades or peels quickly. Wait until water dropped on the wood absorbs within a minute or two, which can take weeks to months depending on climate and lumber.

Spray alone can leave stain sitting in the texture of rough-sawn pickets and missing the deeper grain, so the fence looks uneven and wears faster. Follow each sprayed section with a brush or roller to work stain in, catch drips and even out the color.
Stopping in the middle of a section

When you pause halfway across a section, the edge dries and the next pass overlaps it, leaving a dark lap line. Work post to post, finish the full height of each section and keep a wet edge. Use posts and gates as natural break points.
Ignoring the bottom of the fence

The bottom few inches take sprinkler spray, splashing rain and contact with soil and mulch, so they fade, grow mildew and rot first. Clean and stain the bottom edges carefully, give end grain an extra coat and pull soil and mulch back so the pickets can dry.
Buying stain by the smooth-wood coverage figure

Rough pickets, two faces, posts and rails add up fast. Buying by the smooth-wood figure leaves you short partway through and causes a color shift where the new batch starts. Use the rough-wood figure, count both sides and the framing, and mix cans before starting.
bottomLine: Ready Seal is the stain most fence owners should buy: it sprays evenly, hides lap marks and fades without peeling. SuperDeck is the paint-store alternative with more color control, Olympic Maximum is the easy big-box value, BEHR Premium Solid Color rescues old and mismatched fences, DEFY Extreme fits low-VOC states, Cabot suits cedar showpieces and Thompson's covers utility fences on a budget. The job itself decides how well any of them works: let new treated wood dry, clean and brighten old fences, buy for rough-wood coverage, work post to post in the shade and back-brush as you go.

faqs.q: What is the best stain for a wood fence?
faqs.a: Ready Seal is the best stain for most wood fences because it sprays on evenly, hides lap marks and fades instead of peeling. Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck offers more color control, Olympic Maximum is a strong big-box value, BEHR Premium Solid Color suits old and mismatched fences, and DEFY Extreme is the top water-based choice.

faqs.q: What is the best fence stain and sealer in one?
faqs.a: Ready Seal and Olympic Maximum Stain and Sealant in One are the best combined stain and sealer products for fences. Ready Seal is an oil-based penetrating finish that is very forgiving to spray, while Olympic Maximum is easy to buy and tint at Lowe's. Both add pigment for UV protection and repel water.

faqs.q: Is BEHR fence stain any good?
faqs.a: BEHR Premium Solid Color Waterproofing Stain and Sealer is a good choice for old, patched or mismatched fences because it hides weathering and lasts a long time on vertical boards. Most peeling complaints trace to applying it over an old penetrating stain that still repelled water or onto damp wood, so clean well and let the fence dry first.

faqs.q: What is the best stain for a new fence?
faqs.a: For a new cedar or pressure-treated fence, a penetrating semi-transparent stain such as Ready Seal or DEFY Extreme is the best choice, because it shows the grain and fades evenly. Wait until water dropped on the wood soaks in within a minute or two before staining, which can take weeks for new treated pine.

faqs.q: Which fence stain has the best UV protection?
faqs.a: Pigment is what blocks UV, so solid and well-pigmented semi-transparent stains protect best. Among water-based options, DEFY Extreme adds zinc oxide to its pigment for extra UV resistance. Clear and transparent finishes offer the least sun protection and fade fastest, especially on south and west-facing fence sections.

faqs.q: How long should I wait to stain a new fence?
faqs.a: Wait until the wood absorbs water. New pressure-treated pine often needs several weeks to a few months to dry enough, while kiln-dried treated lumber and cedar can usually be stained sooner. Sprinkle water on a few pickets: if it soaks in within a minute or two the fence is ready, and if it beads, wait.

faqs.q: Should I stain both sides of my fence?
faqs.a: Staining both sides protects the wood more evenly and reduces cupping and warping, because both faces take on and lose moisture at similar rates. If the back faces a neighbor, ask first, since some want to choose their own color. At a minimum, stain the picket tops, posts and any surfaces you can reach on the back.
